title: Heel Thump Test
purpose: Provocation test for syndesmotic (high) ankle sprain by axial impact through the calcaneus.
structure: Anterior and posterior tibiofibular ligaments and interosseous membrane.
procedure: Patient seated with a relaxed ankle (slightly plantarflexed by gravity). Stabilise the lower leg and give a firm thump on the centre of the calcaneus, directing the force along the axis of the tibia.
positive: Pain over the anterior or posterior ankle or in the distal leg (areas of the anterior/posterior tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane). Suggests syndesmotic sprain only once other injuries are excluded by examination and radiographs.

accuracy.source: none; test described by Lindenfeld & Parikh 2005 (Foot Ankle Int) as a clinical tip

notes: Source states the test lacks evidence and is of questionable clinical utility. Return to play after syndesmotic sprain may be twice as long as after a usual sprain.

title: Thompson Test
purpose: Detect a complete Achilles tendon rupture (calf squeeze test).
procedure: Patient prone with the lower legs extended and the ankles beyond the edge of the bench. Squeeze the calf with one hand and watch the foot.
positive: Calf compression produces no plantarflexion (an intact tendon plantarflexes the foot); a loss of the resting plantarflexion preload in prone also suggests rupture.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2014 systematic review with meta-analysis (J Athl Train); primary data Maffulli 1998

notes: High clinical value to confirm and exclude rupture. 66% of Achilles ruptures are asymptomatic before rupture, yet 98% show degenerative pathology. Companion tests: Matles, gap palpation, Copeland.

title: Matles Test
purpose: Detect Achilles tendon rupture by observing resting foot position with the knee flexed (knee flexion test).
procedure: Patient prone, asked to flex both knees to 90 degrees. Observe the position of both feet.
positive: The affected foot falls into neutral or dorsiflexion; with an intact tendon the foot stays slightly plantarflexed.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2014 meta-analysis (J Athl Train); primary data Maffulli 1998; test described by Matles 1975

notes: Source: at least moderate clinical value; likelihood ratios shift post-test probability moderately but the included study had a fairly high risk of bias.

title: Gap Palpation Test
purpose: Detect Achilles tendon rupture by palpating a gap in the tendon.
procedure: Patient supine. Gently palpate along the whole course of the Achilles tendon.
positive: A palpable gap in the continuity of the tendon.

accuracy.source: Maffulli 1998 (Am J Sports Med), the only study; via Reiman et al. 2014 meta-analysis

notes: Source: at least moderate clinical value; fairly high risk of bias in the single study. Source spells the author 'Mafulli' in the text.

title: Copeland Test
purpose: Detect Achilles tendon rupture using a sphygmomanometer cuff on the calf.
procedure: Patient prone with the affected leg over the edge of the bench. Place a blood-pressure cuff around the mid-calf and inflate it to 100 mmHg with the ankle passively plantarflexed. Then dorsiflex the ankle and watch the pressure.
positive: Intact tendon: pressure rises by about 35-60 mmHg. Ruptured tendon: little or no pressure rise.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2014 meta-analysis (J Athl Train); primary data Maffulli 1998

notes: Source: rather weak clinical value (only sensitivity available, high risk of bias).

title: Arc Test
purpose: Detect midportion Achilles tendinopathy and distinguish tendon-body pathology from tendon-sheath irritation (tenosynovitis/paratenonitis).
structure: Achilles tendon midportion (2-6 cm above the calcaneal insertion) and its sheath.
procedure: Patient prone with the ankles clear of the table. Palpate the tendon distal to proximal 2-6 cm above the insertion, squeezing between index finger and thumb for localised thickening. Keep the fingers on the swelling while the patient dorsiflexes and plantarflexes the ankle. If no swelling is found, palpate 3 cm proximal to the insertion during movement. A stethoscope can help detect crepitus.
positive: Tendinopathy of the tendon body: the swelling moves with the tendon during dorsi/plantarflexion. Sheath pathology: the thickening stays relatively still with palpable crepitus.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2014 meta-analysis (J Athl Train), ultrasound reference standard

notes: Source gives a rather weak clinical value: included studies used ultrasound as gold standard and many asymptomatic tendons show pathology. Differential diagnoses listed: retrocalcaneal bursitis, painful os trigonum, tarsal tunnel syndrome, sural neuritis. Companion test: Royal London Hospital test.

title: Royal London Hospital Test
structure: Achilles tendon: midportion (2-5 cm from the insertion) or insertion.
procedure: Patient sitting with the foot over the edge of the bench, ankle neutral or slightly plantarflexed. Palpate the tendon for the tender spot. Patient moves into maximal dorsiflexion; palpate the same spot again. Patient moves into maximal plantarflexion; palpate again.
positive: The tenderness found at rest disappears in maximal dorsiflexion.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2014 meta-analysis (J Athl Train)

notes: Source: at most moderate clinical value (mixed risk of bias). The original authors offer no explanation for why pain disappears under maximal tension. Typical history: morning pain that warms up with activity, after a sudden spike in load.

title: Windlass Test
structure: Plantar fascia (windlass mechanism), first metatarsophalangeal joint.
procedure: Patient stands on a stool or chair with the metatarsal heads resting on the edge and weight on the leg. Passively dorsiflex (extend) the big toe.
positive: Pain or increased pain at the plantar fascia (source: at its insertion near the head of the first metatarsal). Inability to extend the MTP joint may indicate hallux rigidus.

accuracy.source: De Garceau et al. 2003 (Foot Ankle Int)

notes: Not useful to exclude, very useful to confirm plantar fasciitis. Consider the navicular drop test for over-pronation as a contributing factor.

title: Navicular Drop Test
purpose: Quantify pes planus / over-pronation as the navicular tuberosity drops from subtalar neutral to relaxed standing.
structure: Navicular tuberosity, subtalar joint, medial longitudinal arch.
procedure: Palpate and mark the navicular tuberosity. With the patient sitting or standing, bring the talus (subtalar joint) into neutral and mark the height of the tuberosity from the floor on a card. Then let the patient bear weight in relaxed stance and mark the height again.
positive: Difference of at least 1 cm = excessive navicular drop / over-pronation.

accuracy.source: n/a (measurement, not a diagnostic test). Reliability: Picciano et al. 1993 (JOSPT)

notes: Increased navicular drop is associated with overuse injuries: medial tibial stress syndrome, plantar fasciitis, patellofemoral pain. Companion: windlass test; tibialis posterior strengthening for flat feet.

title: Tinel Sign Ankle
purpose: Nerve percussion sign for nerve entrapment at the ankle, including tarsal tunnel syndrome.
structure: Anterior tibial branch of the deep peroneal nerve (anterior to the medial malleolus); tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel.
procedure: The page states the sign can be elicited at two places around the ankle and describes the first: tap anterior to the medial malleolus over the anterior tibial branch of the deep peroneal nerve.
positive: Tingling/paraesthesia in the distribution of the nerve on tapping (standard Tinel interpretation; the page does not spell out the criterion).

accuracy.source: Schwieterman et al. 2013 systematic review (Int J Sports Phys Ther)

notes: ⚠ The page says the sign is elicited at two sites but only describes the anterior site (deep peroneal nerve); the tibial nerve site behind the medial malleolus, which is the classic tarsal tunnel site, is not described in the text. Companion tests: triple compression stress test, dorsiflexion-eversion test. Reference list also includes Oloff & Schulhofer 1998 on flexor hallucis longus dysfunction.

title: Dorsiflexion Eversion Test
purpose: Provocation test for tarsal tunnel syndrome (tibial nerve compression).
structure: Posterior tibial nerve and branches in the tarsal tunnel (under deep fascia, flexor retinaculum, within abductor hallucis).
procedure: Patient side-lying so the tibial nerve is accessible behind the medial malleolus. Maximally dorsiflex the ankle, maximally evert the foot and maximally extend the toes at the MTP joints; hold 5-10 seconds while palpating the tibial nerve for tenderness.
positive: Increase in tenderness over the nerve. Increased pain or numbness should not be scored positive (lower sensitivity for those outcomes).

accuracy.source: Kinoshita et al. 2001 (J Bone Joint Surg Am), single study

notes: High clinical value when scored on tenderness, but only one study so far. Source writes 'MCP joints' for the toe joints (metatarsophalangeal, MTP).

title: Triple Compression Stress Test
purpose: Provocation test for tarsal tunnel syndrome.
structure: Posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel.
procedure: Patient supine. Maximally plantarflex the ankle, bring the foot and heel into maximal inversion and compress the posterior tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus with the fingers for 30 seconds.
positive: Numbness, paraesthesia or pain in the toes, ball of the foot and/or heel.
notes: Source: high clinical value to confirm and exclude tarsal tunnel syndrome, but only one study. Source writes the sensitivity as '85,9%' (comma decimal).

title: Fulcrum Test Tibia
purpose: Screen for medial tibial stress fracture (vs medial tibial stress syndrome) in athletes and military populations.
structure: Medial tibial cortex at the midshaft.
procedure: Patient supine. Place your knee against the lateral border of the lower leg at the tibial midshaft as a fulcrum. Grip the inside of the lower leg just below the knee with one hand and just above the ankle with the other, and forcefully press the tibia against your knee, producing tension on the medial cortex.
positive: Pain reproduced at the medial tibia.

accuracy.source: Milgrom et al. 2021 (J Sci Med Sport)

notes: Weak as a stand-alone test according to the source. Companion tests: hop test (tibia), fulcrum test (hip/femur). Absolute rest may be indicated to prevent progression to a frank cortical fracture.

title: Hop Test
purpose: Screen for medial tibial stress fracture.
procedure: Patient stands barefoot on the affected leg (if both tibias are symptomatic, start with the less symptomatic side) and hops in place as high as possible. Repeat on the uninvolved leg.
positive: Pain reproduced at the tibia on hopping (the page does not state the criterion explicitly; implied by the screening use).

accuracy.source: Milgrom et al. 2021 (J Sci Med Sport), the only study

notes: Source: highly effective to rule out tibial stress fracture; moderate clinical value for now because only one study exists. ⚠ The page does not state what counts as positive. Companion tests: fulcrum test (tibia), fulcrum test (hip).

title: Plantar Fascia Stretch
purpose: Tissue-specific plantar fascia stretch for plantar fasciitis / chronic heel pain.
procedure: Cross the affected leg over the other leg, place the fingers across the base of the toes and pull the toes back towards the shin until a stretch is felt in the arch. Palpate the fascia with the other hand to confirm tension. Hold 10 seconds, about 10 repetitions, 3 times a day.

accuracy.source: n/a (treatment). DiGiovanni et al. 2003 RCT (J Bone Joint Surg Am): plantar-specific stretch superior to standard Achilles stretch at 8 weeks

notes: Rathleff et al. 2014 compared this stretch with high-load strength training: both effective, high-load superior (see 'best exercise for plantar fasciitis'). ⚠ Rathleff is cited in the text but not listed in the page's references.

title: Best Exercise for Plantar Fasciitis
purpose: High-load strength training for plantar fasciitis using the windlass mechanism plus Achilles loading.
structure: Plantar fascia (collagen type 1), Achilles tendon / calf.
procedure: Stand on a step or pedestal with a rolled towel under the toes so that all MTP joints are dorsiflexed (the page notes its own video only dorsiflexes the 1st MTP); hold a chair for balance. Heel raise: 3 s concentric, 2 s hold at the top, 3 s eccentric. Start 3 x 12 every other day for 2 weeks; then 4 x 10 with a backpack of books for 4 weeks; then 5 x 8 with more weight, adding load as strength improves. Start bilateral if single-leg form is not yet possible.
positive: n/a (treatment). Slight pain during exercise is acceptable; worsening after exercise or in the next 24 h should be reported.

accuracy.source: n/a (treatment). Rathleff et al. RCT with 12-month follow-up (Scand J Med Sci Sports; text says 2014, reference says 2015)

notes: Rationale: collagen type 1 responds to high tensile load with increased synthesis, which may normalise degenerative change. ⚠ Text cites Rathleff et al. 2014 while the reference list gives 2015 (e-publication vs print year).

title: Tibialis Posterior Strengthening
purpose: Selective strengthening exercise for tibialis posterior in painful pes planus / tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction.
structure: Tibialis posterior muscle and tendon (dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch).
procedure: Patient sits on a bench, knees about an arm's length apart and flexed about 80 degrees, stabilising the leg with the contralateral forearm between the knees reinforced by the ipsilateral hand. Loop an elastic band around the medial-distal foot at full tension and a 45-degree inclination. Keeping the foot on the floor, the patient slides the forefoot from full abduction into adduction; mark the range with tape to ensure full ROM each repetition. Progress by band tension or a stronger band; Kulig et al. 2009 used 3 x 15, twice a day, for 10 weeks.

accuracy.source: n/a (exercise). Kulig et al. 2004 (MRI activation study), 2005 (orthoses increase activation in pes planus), 2009 (10-week programme reduced pain, improved function)

notes: Kulig 2004 (MRI) found this exercise gives the greatest selective tibialis posterior activation; in flat-footed patients activation is higher with orthoses and shoes, so train with insoles and footwear. Recommended next to foot orthoses in painful pes planus. See navicular drop test for assessing over-pronation.
